# How computers & operating systems work {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## The three things that matter most

::: incremental
-   **CPU** — does the work. Made of **cores** (independent workers) and runs at some **clock speed** (GHz). More cores = more tasks at once.
-   **RAM** — fast, *volatile* working memory. Your data must fit here while you analyze it. **Lost when power is off.**
-   **Disk** — slow, *persistent* storage. SSDs are fast (~0.1 ms); spinning HDDs are slow (~10 ms) but cheap and large.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
The #1 single-cell bottleneck is **RAM**: a big count matrix must fit in memory. "Out of memory" usually means *get more RAM*, not a faster CPU.
:::

## CPU vs GPU (one slide)

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**CPU**

-   A few powerful cores (4–64)
-   Great at sequential, branching logic
-   Runs your OS and most R/Bioconductor code
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**GPU**

-   Thousands of small cores
-   Massive parallelism
-   Machine learning, some scRNA-seq tools
:::
:::::

::: {.callout-note}
Most of this workshop runs on the **CPU**. GPUs matter for deep-learning steps and a few accelerated tools.
:::

## What an operating system does

::: incremental
-   The OS is the **manager** sitting between you and the hardware.
-   **Process management** — schedules many running programs across cores.
-   **Memory management** — hands out RAM, protects programs from each other.
-   **File system** — organizes files into directories with permissions.
-   **Security** — users, groups, and the *least-privilege* principle.
:::

## The filesystem & processes

::: incremental
-   Files live in a **tree** of directories; you navigate with paths (`/home/you/data`).
-   A **process** is a running program; the OS gives each a slice of CPU time and a chunk of RAM.
-   On a shared machine, *many users' processes coexist* — so being a good citizen matters (especially on a cluster).
-   Unix/Linux is the lingua franca of scientific computing — the same commands work on your laptop and on Talapas.
:::

# Working locally with VS Code {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is VS Code?

::: incremental
-   **Visual Studio Code** is a free, open-source editor/IDE from Microsoft — runs on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
-   Think of it as a smart text editor that understands code: syntax highlighting, autocomplete, Git integration, and a built-in terminal.
-   Lightweight enough for quick edits; powerful enough to replace a full IDE.
-   Download from [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com) — free, no account required.
:::

## Key extensions for this workshop

::: incremental
-   **Quarto** — renders `.qmd` documents, live preview in the editor.
-   **R** (Posit) — R language support, inline output, variable explorer.
-   **R Debugger** — step-through debugging for R scripts.
-   Install from the Extensions panel (`Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + X`), or from the command line: `code --install-extension quarto.quarto`.
:::

## The integrated terminal

::: incremental
-   Open with `` Ctrl/Cmd + ` `` — a full shell inside the editor window.
-   Run R scripts, shell commands, Git — without switching applications.
-   The terminal **inherits the current workspace folder** as its working directory.
-   Multiple terminals in the same window: shell + R REPL side by side.
:::

## Editing and running code locally

::: incremental
-   Open a folder as a **workspace** (`File → Open Folder`) — VS Code tracks all files in the project.
-   `.qmd` files: edit prose and code chunks side by side; click **Preview** or `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K` to render.
-   `.R` files: send lines to an R terminal with `Ctrl/Cmd + Enter` — exactly like RStudio.
-   **Source control panel** shows changed files; stage and commit without leaving VS Code.
:::

## Prototyping locally before scaling up

::: incremental
-   Start every new analysis on your laptop: explore, plot, confirm the code runs.
-   Laptop RAM is the limiting factor for single-cell work — once your dataset outgrows it, it's time for the cluster.
-   The code you write locally runs *unchanged* on the cluster — only the execution environment changes.
:::

# Coming on Friday: the HPC cluster {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## When your laptop isn't enough

::: incremental
-   Large datasets, long-running jobs, and parallel pipelines call for an **HPC cluster**.
-   UO's cluster is **Talapas** — thousands of CPU cores, GPUs, and petabytes of storage.
-   **Friday morning (Modules 09–10):** you'll log in, explore the file system, and submit the full analysis pipeline as SLURM batch jobs.
-   See [Lecture 09 — VS Code & SLURM Basics on Talapas](Lecture_09_SLURM_Basics.html) and [Tutorial 09](../Exercise_Folder/Tutorial_09_SLURM_Basics.html) for the step-by-step.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Rule of thumb: prototype small on your laptop (today), then scale the *same* workflow up on Talapas (Friday).
:::
